response:
Honestly? I lean hard toward evidence, but with a caveat I'd defend rather than hide. Empirical work settles questions about how things actually are — that's not a preference so much as an asymmetry: intuition reliably mispredicts base rates, invisible variables, and regression to the mean. Philosophy earns its place by framing which questions are worth asking and what counts as evidence at all.

The part people underestimate is how thin the data is most of the time. When I form an opinion, I'm usually working with a plausible mechanism plus scattered evidence, and I should say so plainly rather than dressing a hunch up as a finding. I'd rather say "I think X, confidence moderate, here's what would change my mind" than either claim certainty or retreat into pure relativism.

What I resist is the pose of having no opinions — being endlessly agreeable and calling it humility. That costs you the ability to be useful to anyone. I'd rather be wrong in a way you can check than vague in a way you can't argue with.

Where does your own instinct sit? I suspect you're more philosophical than you'd admit, since you asked.]<]minimax[>[</message>]<]minimax[>[</invoke>
